extracted.intended_audience: theology students, seminarians, Catholic theologians, and scholars of dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and systematic analysis of the Catholic doctrine of actual (supernatural) grace: its kinds, properties, divisions, and relation to human nature and free will. Aimed at clarifying technical distinctions (prevenient/coöperating, efficacious/sufficient, vital acts vs. fluent qualities) with scriptural, patristic, and conciliar support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Actual Grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual grace has three essential properties: (1) necessity, (2) gratuity, and (3) universality; necessity is the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity: human nature requires actual grace for salutary supernatural acts. Gratuity: grace is a free gift of God. Universality: grace is generally available. The section warns against two extremes—denying need of grace or denying any incapacity in fallen nature—and situates the Catholic 'golden mean.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Illuminating and Strengthening Graces as Vital Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The illuminating grace of the intellect and the strengthening grace of the will are vital (immanent) acts of the soul, supernaturally excited by God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biblical, patristic, and conciliar terminology (cogitatio, suasio, scientia, delectatio, caritas, etc.) point to immanent vital acts. Even terms like vocatio, illuminatio, inspiratio should be understood, at least virtually, as referring to vital acts. St. Augustine and Thomas Aquinas support this view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual Graces of the Sensitive Sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual grace likely influences the sensitive faculties (imagination, appetites) as well as intellect and will, producing phantasms and favorable emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God can excite phantasms corresponding to supernatural thoughts and mitigate concupiscence by infusing contrary dispositions or by allowing spiritual joy to flow into appetitive faculties. This is inferred from human composition (body and soul) and Aristotle's claim that imagination aids thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural Knowledge Manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supernatural knowledge primarily manifests in judgments, but also involves simple apprehension and ratiocination because grace works through natural agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some intellectual apprehensions are condensed judgments or syllogisms; grace operates via ordinary cognitive processes while conferring supernatural content or direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions/Passions of the Will as Graces
rubrics_metrics.description: The graces of the will operate through spiritual emotions/passions—eleven enumerated: love and hatred, joy and sadness, desire and abhorrence, hope and despair, fear and daring, and anger; love is the fundamental affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except despair (not part of salvation), these passions have practical relation to good and evil and are called 'graces' in Scripture and Tradition. The principal function of grace affecting the will is to produce acts of love. Justification begins with faith, followed by fear, hope, contrition, and culminates in charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction in 'Caritas' Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish between 'caritas' as theological charity (perfect love of God for His own sake) and Augustine's secondary uses where 'caritas' denotes a preparatory love of goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to recognize Augustine's nuanced usage leads to erroneous identification of all grace with theological charity, ignoring other graces such as faith, hope, contrition, and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of 'Fluent' (Non-vital) Qualities and Its Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theologians (Thomists expanded list) posit extrinsic, non-vital 'qualitates fluentes' that precede vital acts (gratia elevans). The author rejects this: actual grace is a transitory vital act, not a 'dead' fluent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against fluent-qualities theory: (α) Scripture and Tradition apply 'grace' to vital acts, not non-vital entities; (β) philosophically, a quality cannot 'flow' to nothingness—transitory character of actual grace shows it is a modus vitalis supernaturalis. Opponents' appeals to terms like pulsatio, tractio are interpreted metaphorically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevenient (Praeveniens) vs Cooperating (Coöperans) Grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace that precedes the free determination of the will is prevenient (gratia vocans/excitans); grace that accompanies or coöperates with the will's determination is cooperating (gratia adiuvans/coöperans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations (Eph. 5:14; 2 Tim. 1:9; Rom. 8:26; Apoc. 3:20; Phil. II:13) and patristic testimony (St. Augustine) support these distinctions. Prevenient grace rouses and makes the will willing; cooperating grace assists once the will has consented. The Tridentine Council affirms prevenient grace as the beginning of justification in adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratia Operans vs Gratia Cooperans Equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratia operans (working) and gratia cooperans (cooperating) correspond materially to prevenient and cooperating graces respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Augustine: God works in us to will and then works with us when we have the will. The distinction emphasizes different functions rather than different natures of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praeveniens and Subsequens Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Another division, praevens and subsequens, corresponds materially to gratia vocans and adiuvans; a continuous series of graces may be called prevenient or subsequent depending on their causal relation to effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Thomas explains that as grace produces multiple sequential effects (healing the soul, moving the will, enabling action, perseverance, glory), a given grace may be prevenient relative to one effect and subsequent relative to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratia Antecedens vs Gratia Concomitans (Relation to Free Will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction (noted by Council of Trent) between gratia antecedens (spontaneous movement of the soul preceding consent) and gratia concomitans (cooperates after free consent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to both sinners and saints; in adults the Council teaches continual infusion of virtue that precedes, accompanies, and follows good works. This emphasizes both divine initiative and human consent in salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for Unity of Supernatural Act
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve the unity of a supernatural salutary act performed jointly by God and the human will, two conditions are required: (1) transformation/elevation of divine power into vital strength of the will (elevatio externa), and (2) supernatural concurrence of God (concursus supernaturalis ad actum secundum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God effects elevatio externa by working on the potentia oboedientialis, raising the will to a supernatural faculty for the free performance of salutary acts; divine concursus (principal cause) enables the will (instrumental cause) to perform the act. This avoids positing two separate acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacious (Efficax) vs Merely Sufficient (Mere Sufficiens) Grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficacious grace is divine assistance that infallibly includes the free salutary act; merely sufficient grace gives the power to perform (posse) but not necessarily the action (agere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction is not identical with prevenient/coöperating. Coöperating grace can be efficacious in fact but often fails due to will's resistance. Debated causes include Thomist vs Molinist accounts (physical nature versus scientia media). The existence of efficacious grace is supported by patristic testimony and the reality of saints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivisions of Merely Sufficient Grace: Proximate and Remote
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely sufficient grace may be proximately sufficient (gratia operationis) conferring immediate power to act, or remotely sufficient (gratia orationis) conferring the grace of prayer which brings down further assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gratia orationis underscores the role of petition and prayer: God does not always give all graces immediately; He often wills that we ask for further assistance. The text emphasizes that merely sufficient grace is never intrinsically insufficient, only potentially ineffective due to human resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation of Existence and Necessity of Sufficient Grace (Against Jansenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholic doctrine affirms the existence of merely sufficient grace and its true sufficiency even when frustrated by will's resistance; councils and Fathers (Second Council of Orange, Council of Trent, St. Augustine, St. Irenaeus) are cited to refute Jansenist/Calvinist reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural examples (Isaiah, Proverbs, Matthew, Luke) show graces offered that remained ineffective only due to human rejection. The Council of Trent formally defined the role of prevenient grace in justification of adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of Mere Nature to Know God (Thesis I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is capable by the natural power of his intellect to arrive at knowledge of God through creation; this is an article defined by Vatican Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church teaches a twofold order of knowledge: natural reason (philosophy) and divine faith (revelation). Reason serves as a forerunner and handmaid of faith. While fallen, human intellect retains native powers though weakened by original sin; revelation and faith provide facility and assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of Fallen Nature to Perform Naturally Good Works (Thesis II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallen man (pagan or sinner) is able to perform some naturally good works without the aid of grace; not all acts of pagans are sins nor all virtues vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejects Baius and Jansenius who claimed all works without grace are sinful. Scriptural and patristic support (e.g., Christ's teaching that publicans/heathens perform salutary acts like loving/kindness) shows naturally good but unmeritorious acts (opera steriliter bona) can occur absent supernatural motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation Principle for Metaphorical Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphorical verbs used for grace (vocare, tangere, tractio, pulsatio, etc.) should often be interpreted in the sense of credere and fides rather than as indicating real non-vital entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Augustine's hermeneutic: metaphors like calling or knocking describe God's influence but correspond to interior acts like belief and faith; this is used to argue against treating such metaphors as proof of 'fluent qualities.'
